title: Faith rises and falls
hook: many scholars teach that iman increases with good deeds and decreases with sins

segments.voice: Yesterday, qadar, the sixth article, and your line: all by his decree. When an if only started up, did you swap it for it happened? Day one thousand two hundred forty.

Phone batteries have a little icon in the corner. Full, then less, then a red sliver, then you plug it in and watch it climb. The six articles of faith from this week could sound like a list you either have or don't, like a membership card. But the Qur'an and the hadith talk about iman more like that battery. It can be more. It can be less. It can be topped up. Today closes the week on the six articles, and not with a seventh thing to believe: a way of holding the six.
screen: `A BATTERY ICON.` → `MORE, LESS, TOPPED UP.` → `A WAY OF HOLDING THE SIX.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. The Qur'an speaks of Allah sending peace into the hearts of believers, in Pickthall's words, "that they might add faith unto their faith." Add faith to faith. So faith, in that verse, is something that can grow. Another verse says that when Allah's revelations are recited to believers, their faith increases. Second, the branches. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says iman has many branches. The highest is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. The lowest is moving something harmful out of the road. And modesty, the hadith adds, is a branch of faith too. So on this picture, faith isn't only in the head. It reaches all the way down to a rock in the street. Third, the scholars. Al-Bukhari titled a chapter in his collection on how faith increases and decreases, and a line of Sunni scholars teaches exactly that: good deeds raise it, sins lower it. Hanafi and Maturidi scholars put it another way. For them, the core of iman, the belief itself, doesn't get bigger or smaller, but its light and its fruits in a person's life do. Both views are held within Sunni Islam. Last, why it matters. If faith can fall, a low day isn't the end of anything. And if it can rise, the way back up is small and concrete: one branch, one deed, one rock moved out of the road.
screen: `ADD FAITH UNTO THEIR FAITH.` · `FROM THE TESTIMONY TO THE ROAD.` · `TWO WAYS SCHOLARS DESCRIBE IT.` · then, large: `ONE ROCK OUT OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The practice: do one deed to raise it. You'll do the deed after the bell; for now, choose it. Think of the lowest branch in the hadith: moving something harmful out of the way. Where is that for you today? A box blocking a hallway. A sharp comment you could take out of a conversation. A task left in someone else's path. Pick one, small and real. Picture yourself doing it, start to finish. If you pray, you can ask that it be accepted. If you don't, simply decide. The bell holds the time.
Faith rises and falls. The teaching that iman can be added to by good deeds and lessened by sins; in the Qur'an's words, faith added to faith. Today's word.

Your line: faith grows. Today, do the deed you chose, and notice the battery icon afterward. The six are done; tomorrow the theologians begin, with speaking about Allah. Day one thousand two hundred forty.

howItsDone: In Muslim teaching, faith is spoken of as rising and falling, with good deeds, prayer and Qur'an recitation as ways to strengthen it; Hanafi and Maturidi scholars hold that the core of belief stays constant while its strength and fruits vary.

fork.setup: what does the hadith in Sahih Muslim call the lowest branch of faith?
options: moving something harmful out of the road.
fork.reveal: the highest branch is the testimony, and the lowest is moving harm out of the road. faith reaches all the way down to the street.

trapdoor: what you thought: you either have faith or you don't.
what it means: iman can grow with good deeds and shrink with sins; the Qur'an speaks of faith added to faith.
what a scholar hears: al-Bukhari's chapter on faith increasing and decreasing, the branches hadith, and the Hanafi-Maturidi view that the core of belief is constant.
